Milestone Submission - Music Recommendation System¶

Music streaming platforms need to surface relevant songs from large catalogs to retain users. This project builds a recommendation system on the Million Song Dataset to predict what songs a user is likely to listen to based on past play counts.¶

In this exercise, the objective is to build and evaluate recommendation systems that better predict the interaction between users and songs. The process will follow these steps:¶

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA): Explore and visualize the data to uncover patterns, distributions, and key statistics that inform the modeling approach.

Data Quality & Preprocessing: Identify and address any anomalies, missing values, or inconsistencies to ensure the data is clean and reliable.

Building Recommendation Systems: Develop multiple recommendation models using different techniques — including popularity-based, collaborative filtering, matrix factorization, and content-based approaches.

Model Evaluation: Test and compare the performance of each model using appropriate metrics such as Precision@K, Recall@K, F1 Score, and RMSE.

Conclusions & Recommendations: Based on model performance, draw conclusions on the most effective approach and provide recommendations on model selection, as well as any improvements to data collection or processing that could further enhance prediction quality.

Exploring the dataset and performing EDA¶

Why these cutoff thresholds? A user cutoff of 90 and a song cutoff of 120 and a play count of less than or equal to 5 were applied to filter out users and songs with very few interactions. Keeping low-interaction records would result in an extremely sparse user-item interaction matrix, making the models computationally expensive and reducing prediction quality. These thresholds strike a balance between retaining enough data (130,398 observations) for meaningful model training while ensuring every user and song has sufficient interaction history to compute reliable similarity scores.

def top_nsongs(data, n, min_interaction = 100):
    recommendations = data[data['Count'] > min_interaction]
    recommendations = recommendations.sort_values(by = 'avg_songs', ascending = False)
    return recommendations.index[:n]

Why these five techniques?¶

The five models chosen cover the full spectrum of recommendation approaches and are well suited to this dataset's characteristics. The rank-based model handles cold-start users with no history. User-User and Item-Item collaborative filtering exploit the moderate interaction density (10–40 songs per user) to find meaningful similarity signals. SVD matrix factorization handles the sparsity of the 1.8M possible interaction space more efficiently than neighborhood methods by learning compact latent representations. Content-based filtering provides a fallback for new songs with no play history by leveraging the available metadata. Together these five approaches ensure every user and every song can receive a recommendation regardless of their interaction history.

Model 2: User-user similarity neighborhood based collaborative filtering¶

for this model, we will find users who are similar to the current user using cosine, or MSD distance, then recommend what those similar user liked. then we can tune the model with GridSearchCV over K(neighbors), the downside for this approach is the performance with new or rare users could be weak as there will be challenging to calculate the MSD or Cosine distance

Next, i will create a useful function to take the recommendation model as input and gives the precision@k, recall@k and F-1score@k for that model - these metrics will show if the relevant item is recommended item, and if the recommended item is relevant, in addition, for F-1 score to measure the accuracy of the model.

In [32]:
def precision_recall_at_k(model, k = 30, threshold = 1.5):
    """Return precision and recall at k metrics for each user"""

    # First map the predictions to each user.
    user_est_true = defaultdict(list)

    #Making predictions on the test data
    predictions = model.test(testset)

    for uid, _, true_r, est, _ in predictions:
        user_est_true[uid].append((est, true_r))

    precisions = dict()
    recalls = dict()
    for uid, playing_count in user_est_true.items():

        # Sort play count by estimated value
        playing_count.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True)

        # Number of relevant items
        n_rel = sum((true_r >= threshold) for (_, true_r) in playing_count)

        # Number of recommended items in top k
        n_rec_k = sum((est >= threshold) for (est, _) in playing_count[:k])

        # Number of relevant and recommended items in top k
        n_rel_and_rec_k = sum(((true_r >= threshold) and (est >= threshold))
                              for (est, true_r) in playing_count[:k])

        # Precision@K: Proportion of recommended items that are relevant
        # When n_rec_k is 0, Precision is undefined. We here set Precision to 0 when n_rec_k is 0.

        precisions[uid] = n_rel_and_rec_k / n_rec_k if n_rec_k != 0 else 0

        # Recall@K: Proportion of relevant items that are recommended
        # When n_rel is 0, Recall is undefined. We here set Recall to 0 when n_rel is 0.

        recalls[uid] = n_rel_and_rec_k / n_rel if n_rel != 0 else 0

    #Mean of all the predicted precisions are calculated.
    precision = round((sum(prec for prec in precisions.values()) / len(precisions)),3)
    #Mean of all the predicted recalls are calculated.
    recall = round((sum(rec for rec in recalls.values()) / len(recalls)),3)

    accuracy.rmse(predictions)
    print('Precision: ', precision) #Command to print the overall precision
    print('Recall: ', recall) #Command to print the overall recall
    print('F_1 score: ', round((2*precision*recall)/(precision+recall),3))

Prediction(uid=6958, iid=1671, r_ui=2, est=1.976516019592846, details={'actual_k': 40, 'was_impossible': False})

the model successfully found 40 similar neighbors (actual_k: 40) to base the estimate on. The predicted play count is 1.98 against the actual of 2.00, a variance of only 0.02 — a solid result that reflects genuine user-neighbor similarity rather than a global mean fallback. This gives us more confidence in the model's personalization ability, and we will next explore GridSearchCV to see if tuning the number of neighbors and similarity measure can further tighten this variance.

def get_recommendations(data, user_id, top_n, algo):

    # Creating an empty list to store the recommended song ids
    recommendations = []

    # Creating an user item interactions matrix
    user_item_interactions_matrix = data.pivot(index = 'user_id', columns = 'song_id', values = 'play_count')

    # Extracting those song IDs which the user ID has not interacted yet
    non_interacted_songs = user_item_interactions_matrix.loc[user_id][user_item_interactions_matrix.loc[user_id].isnull()].index.tolist()

    # Looping through each of the song IDs which user ID has not interacted yet
    for item_id in non_interacted_songs:

        # Predicting the ratings for those non interacted song IDs by this user
        est = algo.predict(user_id, item_id).est

        # Appending the predicted ratings
        recommendations.append((item_id, est))

    # Sorting the predicted ratings in descending order
    recommendations.sort(key = lambda x: x[1], reverse = True)

    # Returing top n highest predicted rating songs for this user
    return recommendations[:top_n]

def ranking_songs(recommendations, final_rating):
    # Sort the songs based on playing count
    ranked_songs = final_rating.loc[[items[0] for items in recommendations]].sort_values('Count', ascending=False)[['Count']].reset_index()
    
    # Merge with recommended songs to get predicted ratings
    ranked_songs = ranked_songs.merge(  
        pd.DataFrame(recommendations, columns=['song_id', 'predicted_ratings']),
        on='song_id', how='inner'
    )
    
    # Corrected ratings formula - needs parentheses around the fraction
    ranked_songs['corrected_ratings'] = ranked_songs['predicted_ratings'] - (1 / np.sqrt(ranked_songs['Count']))
    
    # Sort based on corrected ratings
    ranked_songs = ranked_songs.sort_values('corrected_ratings', ascending=False)  
    
    return ranked_songs

Model 4: Based Collaborative Filtering - Matrix Factorization¶

Model-based Collaborative Filtering is a personalized recommendation system, the recommendations are based on the past behavior of the user and it is not dependent on any additional information. We use latent features to find recommendations for each user.¶

Building a baseline matrix factorization recommendation system¶

In [61]:
svd = SVD(random_state = 1)

svd.fit(trainset)

precision_recall_at_k(svd)

RMSE: 1.0152
Precision:  0.4
Recall:  0.587
F_1 score:  0.476

The SVD baseline delivers Recall (0.587) and F1 (0.476), and RMSE of 1.015, not so different from the other models, lets sample test and optimize

In [83]:
svd.predict(6958, 1671, r_ui = 2, verbose = True)

user: 6958       item: 1671       r_ui = 2.00   est = 1.53   {'was_impossible': False}
Out[83]:
Prediction(uid=6958, iid=1671, r_ui=2, est=1.5347858505827834, details={'was_impossible': False})

The variance is huge comparing to the other models, 2-1.53 = 0.47, lets optimize and test again

The model has overestimated the listens, we will try to fix this by tunning the hyperarameters of the model using GridSearchCV

In [64]:
param_grid = {
    'n_epochs': [10, 20, 30],
    'lr_all': [0.001, 0.005, 0.01],
    'reg_all': [0.1, 0.2, 0.4]
}
# Performing 2-Fold gridsearch cross-validation

Model 5: Cluster Based Recommendation System¶

In clustering-based recommendation systems, we explore the similarities and differences in people's tastes in songs based on how they rate different songs. We cluster similar users together and recommend songs to a user based on play_counts from other users in the same cluster.¶

def get_recommendations(data, user_id, top_n, algo):

    # Creating an empty list to store the recommended song IDs
    recommendations = []

    # Creating an user-item interactions matrix
    user_item_interactions_matrix = data.pivot(index = 'user_id', columns = 'song_id', values = 'play_count')

    # Extracting those songIDs which the userId has not interacted yet
    non_interacted_songs = user_item_interactions_matrix.loc[user_id][user_item_interactions_matrix.loc[user_id].isnull()].index.tolist()

    # Looping through each of the song IDs which userId has not interacted yet
    for item_id in non_interacted_songs:

        # Predicting the ratings for those non interacted song IDs by this user
        est = algo.predict(user_id, item_id).est

        # Appending the predicted ratings
        recommendations.append((item_id, est))

    # Sorting the predicted ratings in descending order
    recommendations.sort(key = lambda x: x[1], reverse = True)

    # Returing top n highest predicted rating songs for this user
    return recommendations[:top_n]

def ranking_songs(recommendations, final_rating):
    # Sort the songs based on playing count
    ranked_songs = final_rating.loc[[items[0] for items in recommendations]].sort_values('Count', ascending=False)[['Count']].reset_index()
    
    # Merge with recommended songs to get predicted ratings
    ranked_songs = ranked_songs.merge(  # was ranked_songs
        pd.DataFrame(recommendations, columns=['song_id', 'predicted_ratings']),
        on='song_id', how='inner'
    )
    
    # Corrected ratings formula - needs parentheses around the fraction
    ranked_songs['corrected_ratings'] = ranked_songs['predicted_ratings'] - (1 / np.sqrt(ranked_songs['Count']))
    
    # Sort based on corrected ratings
    ranked_songs = ranked_songs.sort_values('corrected_ratings', ascending=False)  
    
    return ranked_songs

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

def tokenize(text):
    text = re.sub(r"[^a-zA-Z]", " ", text.lower())
    tokens = word_tokenize(text)
    words = [w for w in tokens if w not in stopwords.words('english')]
    text_lems = [WordNetLemmatizer().lemmatize(lem).strip() for lem in words]
    return text_lems

def recommendations(title, similar_songs):
    recommended_songs = []

    
    idx = indices[indices == title].index[0]

    
    score_series = pd.Series(similar_songs[idx]).sort_values(ascending=False)

    
    top_10_indexes = list(score_series.iloc[1:3].index)

    
    for i in top_10_indexes:
        recommended_songs.append(list(df_small.index)[i])

    return recommended_songs

The top two recommendations — Everlong and The Pretender — are both Foo Fighters tracks, confirming that the TF-IDF vectorizer correctly identified artist name as the strongest similarity signal in the text feature. The model is effectively grouping songs by the same artist together, which is the most intuitive form of content similarity a listener would expect.

Conclusions:¶

The table below summarizes the final performance of all models after applying the play_count ≤ 5 filter, which ensured a consistent and meaningful rating scale across all evaluations:¶

Model RMSE Precision Recall F1
KNN User-User (baseline) 1.0875 0.386 0.619 0.475
KNN User-User (optimized) 1.0365 0.416 0.641 0.505
KNN Item-Item (baseline) 1.0188 0.389 0.532 0.449
KNN Item-Item (optimized) 1.0117 0.403 0.583 0.477
SVD (baseline) 1.0152 0.400 0.587 0.476
SVD (optimized) 1.0214 0.405 0.661 0.502
CoClustering (baseline) 1.0344 0.385 0.563 0.457
CoClustering (optimized) 1.0344 0.385 0.563 0.457
Content-Based — — — —

All models perform within a tight RMSE band of 1.01–1.09, confirming that the play_count filter successfully resolved the rating scale mismatch and produced reliable, comparable predictions across all models

SVD optimized leads on the two most important metrics — Recall (0.661) and F1 (0.502) — making it the strongest overall performer for recommendation purposes

KNN User-User optimized is the strongest neighborhood-based model with the best single prediction variance (0.13) and competitive Recall (0.641), confirming that user similarity is a more powerful signal than item similarity for this dataset - may suggest overfitting

KNN Item-Item optimized achieves the lowest RMSE (1.0117) but consistently underperforms on Recall across both baseline and optimized runs, suggesting item-to-item co-interaction signals are weaker in this catalog - may suggest overfitting

CoClustering showed no improvement after tuning — both baseline and optimized produced identical metrics

Content-Based filtering successfully recommended artist-consistent songs (e.g. Foo Fighters tracks for "Learn To Fly"), validating the TF-IDF approach

Data Insights:¶

The dataset is heavily right-skewed — 55.6% of all user-song interactions have a play count of exactly 1, meaning most listening behaviour is exploratory rather than deeply engaged. This sparsity is the primary driver of moderate Recall scores across all models

The 90/120 cutoff thresholds (minimum 90 interactions per user, 120 per song) were critical for reducing matrix sparsity from 1.7M possible interactions down to 117K observed ones, making the models computationally feasible without sacrificing too much data

Proposed Solution & Recommendations:¶

Recommended model:

SVD (optimized) with parameters n_epochs=30, lr_all=0.001, reg_all=0.1 SVD is recommended as the primary production model for the following reasons: Performance: It achieves the highest Recall (0.661) and F1 (0.502) — the metrics that matter most for a recommendation system where the goal is to surface as many relevant songs as possible within the top-K results. A Recall of 0.661 means the model successfully identifies ~66% of songs a user would genuinely enjoy.

Speed & Computational Efficiency:

SVD completed training in under a minute, while KNN User-User and KNN Item-Item both required several minutes to run — even on this relatively small dataset of 117k interactions. SVD learns a compact set of latent factors through matrix decomposition, which is significantly faster to compute and requires far less memory. On a real-world music platform with millions of users and hundreds of thousands of songs, this difference would be measured in hours versus seconds — making SVD the only practically viable option at scale.

Production Readiness & Interpretability:

The SVD optimized model is ready for production deployment — its RMSE of 1.02 on a 1–5 play count scale represents a prediction error of approximately 1 play unit, which is acceptable for a streaming context.

While SVD's latent factors are not directly interpretable in the way a decision tree would be, the recommendations themselves are fully explainable at the output level — the system can present users with "because you listened to X, we recommend Y", making it interpretable for business stakeholders without exposing the underlying mathematics.

The model's fast training time (under a minute) also means it can be retrained daily on fresh interaction data without significant computational overhead.
